WDS technologies facilitate high-speed connectivity for numerous remote sites within a limited geographic area by utilizing unlicensed licensed bands, specifically IEEE 802.11g and IEEE 802.11n. The research focuses on a dedicated link connecting an IP Camera to the main control center, ensuring the transmitted video maintains a constant Frame Rate (FRI) regardless of site distance. Video quality is quantified using the Full Reference Metric Peak Signal to Noise Ratio (PSNR). Performance was evaluated across various transmission distances, data packet sizes, image resolutions, image compression algorithms, image capture frequencies, and simulated channel bit error rates. All simulations were conducted using MATLAB. The study highlights that for DED2D applications where the transmitter must operate at a constant FRI independent of distance, it is essential to continuously monitor the calculated PSNR to guarantee consistent video quality. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that for short-range nDDED2D channel communications, it is feasible to maintain a constant FRI while achieving acceptable video quality. However, as distance increases beyond the wireless channel's effective range, the system must reduce the input FI to sustain an acceptable PSNR, resulting in fewer video frames per second. Furthermore, it is suggested that for VHI frequencies, nDDED2D systems can achieve higher PSI values over longer distances, whereas 5SI systems perform better at shorter distances. It is also observed that IEEE 802.11n offers superior performance compared to IEEE 802.11g. Finally, the paper emphasizes that for NDED2D systems, it is crucial to be aware of the reduction in video frame count when transmitting over very long distances. Keywords: DED2D, IP Camera, IEEE 802.11g, IEEE 802.11n, MATLAB, NDED2D, PSNR, VHI.

We demonstrate that for any such sentence $\Phi$, there exists a corresponding sentence $\Phi'$ utilizing the same variable count but relying solely on one symmetric binary relation, such that the spectrum of $\Phi'$ is linearly proportional to that of $\Phi$. Furthermore, all models of $\Phi'$ are bipartite graphs. As a consequence, we establish that determining whether a set of cardinalities constitutes a spectrum for sentences with three variables is $\Pi^0_1$-complete, even when restricted to symmetric graphs. Finally, we address the linearity question regarding spectra within the fragment of monotone logic defined by three variables. While it is evident that linearity for a single sentence is a $\Pi^0_1$-complete property, the complexity of linearity for entire spectra remains unresolved. We prove that for the specific fragment of pre-geometric three-variable logic, the problem of deciding linearity for spectra is indeed $\Pi^0_1$-complete. Additionally, we analyze several natural extensions to this result, notably the inclusion of pre-geometric binary relations and equality. For this broader framework, we show that the complexity of the linearity problem remains at $\Pi^0_1$-complete. Furthermore, we investigate spectra among pre-geometric graphs and reveal that, contrary to the simpler scenarios, linearity for such spectra can reach the higher complexity tier of $\Pi^0_1$-complete. Finally, we discuss potential extensions of this result. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any first-order sentence $\Phi$, it is possible to construct a sentence $\Psi$ utilizing the same number of variables but containing exactly one predicate of arity four, ensuring that $\Psi$ admits no pre-geometric interpretations, thereby rendering its spectrum among pre-geometric graphs empty. Consequently, $\Psi$ cannot be expressed as a combination of unary and ternary relations, nor as an intersection of symmetric binary relations.

Utilizing a ray-tracing simulation of an 11-18-11 relativistic ion optical system, we assess the design's potential for high-resolution phase-plate phase-contrast imaging. Our analysis indicates that electrostatic phase plates can achieve resolution limits dictated by aberrations and the phase plate itself, reaching values as low as ~22 nm for 100 keV imaging at a magnification of 100. We demonstrate that appropriate phase plate configurations can simultaneously suppress both spatial incoherence and the highest energy dark-field scattering, effectively addressing the two primary barriers to such resolution. Additionally, we show that carefully engineered phase plates can substantially mitigate ion coherency challenges arising from hyperthermal energy distributions. Finally, we conclude with a discussion on extending these methodologies to other experimental conditions and accelerators. This research establishes a foundation for future electrostatic phase plate designs aimed at both phase-contrast imaging and related applications. Ultimately, electrostatic phase plates hold the potential to become essential instruments for high-resolution imaging using the ADL accelerators. Their application may also prove valuable for other state-of-the-art 100 keV electron microscopes. While they may not yet be critical for most existing microscopes, their utility becomes relevant when pushing towards higher resolutions or considering specialized applications. The accelerated electron microscope certainly offers numerous opportunities for such developments. Furthermore, electrostatic phase plates remain applicable to various other technologies, including high NA microscopes, coherent diffractive imaging, phase-retrieval algorithms, coherent diffractive imaging, electron ptychography, ptychographical diffractive imaging, electron tomography, stochastical ptychography, coherent diffractive imaging, nanoscale tomography, advanced materials research, and more. This paper outlines the accessibility of electrostatic phase plates and provides a roadmap to initiate investigations into novel phase plate designs and their specific applications.

To tackle this limitation, we introduce Fast-PI, a novel non-autoregressive tacotron-style model that generates speech waveforms with prosody continuity using continuous text input. This paper introduces Secure Encryption Neural Networks (SENN), a block-based architecture capable of privately learning DNNs using SENN-encrypted inputs, while producing only these encrypted outputs without revealing any intermediate features. To the best of our knowledge, SENN is the first approach able to train and infer DNNs for practical tasks on encrypted inputs beyond simple boolean functions. We evaluated SENN-encrypted images across various image classification tasks, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, EMNIST, and the private medical dataset PaImD. Results indicate that SENN slightly lags behind state-of-the-art noise-free encryption methods (such as FHE and NVFLARE) in accuracy but significantly surpasses them in efficiency. Consequently, SENN-encrypted images achieve higher accuracy than previously reported AES-encrypted image approaches. We aim for SENN to serve as a vital component in future privacy-preserving DNN applications by offering a compelling trade-off between privacy and efficiency. Additionally, SENN-enhanced data can complement existing encryption schemes to create a multi-layered privacy framework. Our code and implementation are accessible at: https://github.com/pritam129/SENN.

These probes inevitably sample target properties at different length scales dictated by their respective resolutions. Consequently, measuring the same matter using multiple probes generates a vast amount of data that must adhere to universality principles during interpretation. Ultimately, this data enables the construction of physical models representing the target's landscape as seen through each probe. Although a wealth of complementary information is available for the strong-interaction structure of hadrons, no systematic, quantitative analysis has yet been performed. By applying Fluctuation Dissipation and impedance analogies—derived from the Biot-Savart law and Fermi's Golden Rule—we establish a rigorous framework to quantitatively compare the hadron landscape mapped by different probes. This method successfully reconciles seemingly conflicting findings from various experiments and yields several new, testable predictions. In particular, our universal parametrisation offers a powerful and straightforward way to encode the density and compressibility of hadronic material, allowing hadron phenomenology to be understood and predicted using dimensionless variables. Such insights hold significant potential for optimizing the production of hadrons at facilities like the Electron-Ion Collider and the Hadron Solar Neutrino Factory. New collections of experimental data are currently under preparation for these upcoming facilities. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the light hadron landscape as observed by the photon and $\pi^\pm$ probes at the Photon-Exchanged-Pion Interference (PPI) experiment at the former European Muon Collaboration's SLC scattering ring. This analysis is currently in progress and awaiting publication.

Theoretical models propose that magnetic fields facilitate this rapid accretion through mechanisms like magnetic instability, Ruffini-Erdelyi (RE), or the Hoop-Radial (HR) process. This study examines how these magnetic field configurations influence gas dynamics during accretion onto young star systems, with a specific focus on inter-gas interactions. Utilizing RE and HR magnetic field models as input for 2-dimensional Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations, we explore how magnetic forces gas motion, mass accretion rates, and stellar masses across young star system ages. The results indicate that RE and HR fields generate Lorentz forces directed toward the accretor, accelerating inflowing gas and enhancing the efficiency of mass accretion. For systems younger than 3 million years, the total accreted mass under RE and HR scenarios increases significantly, reaching up to 3 orders of magnitude greater than predictions from standard accretion theory. Additionally, magnetic fields promote higher concentration of accreted gas onto the youngest star systems, resulting in brighter luminosities associated with stronger magnetic field strengths. Regarding the specific impact of magnetic forces on inflowing gas, radial components tend to increase the velocity of infalling gas, particularly in RE cases, whereas tangential components generally decelerate gas movement, more commonly observed in HR scenarios. These findings suggest that magnetic fields play a crucial role in the magnetic braking mechanism of young star systems and can resolve the discrepancy between observed and theoretical accretion rates in young stellar clusters, as well as the high rotation rates seen in pre-main sequence stars, provided other factors supporting these claims hold true. These objectives were achieved through a Python program integrating modules for SPH and Magnetic Particle Particle-Particle (M3P) calculations to assess the specific effects of magnetic fields on inter-particle forces and inflowing gas. This specialized code is provided as a supplementary resource to support young star system researchers. Furthermore, to our knowledge, this represents the first application of SPH simulations involving magnetic fields generated by stellar masses. Our findings suggest that gas accretion rates for young star systems could be approximately 3 times higher than current estimates, potentially leading to more luminous T Tauri stars and accelerating the evolution of young star systems, which may have significant implications for galaxy evolution. According to the Eddington Streamlining Instability theory, $\lambda$ should self-regulate near 1; however, observational evidence for this balance remains ambiguous. This study investigates whether high Eddington ratios are linked to rapid accretion states characterized by radio-loudness. Utilizing the 1MAJ radio catalog and stacking techniques across various luminosities within 1MAJ sources, we identify a factor of 3.4 increase in radio power between the Eddington-poor sample (0.01$\le\lambda\le$0.1) and the Eddington-ratio-greater-than-one sample, after controlling for luminosity, redshift, and Eddington ratio. Furthermore, λ=1 sources exhibit median Eddington-limited line luminosities 4.6 times higher than those of the low Eddington ratio group, even when accounting for the larger number of sources and luminosity spread. These findings corroborate the notion that Eddington-mass black holes undergo accretion at or near the Eddington limit, supporting the existence of a self-regulating mechanism in the cosmic population of black holes. Additionally, we observe a strong correlation ($\rho$=0.83) between the Eddington ratio and the Eddington limits of emission lines (e.g., C$\alpha$) when $\lambda>0.1$, indicating that AGN central engines radiate at approximately 0.25 to 0.4 of the Eddington limit using non-thermal radiation. Our results indicate that among Eddington-limited AGNs, 15% possess Eddington masses, with an uncertainty of approximately $\pm$10%. These findings underscore the significance of the fat black hole sequence in the evolution of Eddington-limited black holes. While temporal fluctuations are typically assessed via wavelet analysis, most prior studies lack statistical validation. This study applies Gaussian random field theory to complete the statistical analysis of temporal and spectral variability dynamics. Unlike prior research that models accretion using continuous fluids, this work employs the collisionless Vlasov equation to define the infalling gas. We calculate critical parameters—including the accretion rate, specific energy, and angular momentum—for gas clouds originating from both rest and initial velocities. Our findings reveal that the initial state of the clouds significantly influences these results. This outcome implies that black hole angular momentum following gas accretion may be less predictable than previously thought. Finally, since our black hole accretion results closely mirror those of collapsing kinetic gas clouds, these findings may also illuminate the formation mechanisms of primordial primary and secondary black holes. and photon emission for a neutral, non-relativistic atom in motion, interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a thin, perfectly conducting plane. These findings generalize our previous results for a stationary atom, which emerged from the diagonalization of the total Hamiltonian and accounted for linear responses to an external electric field (stark effect) and the spontaneous decay of an internal transition. The present work demonstrates that the shifted frequencies of de-excitation and emission spectra, along with lifetime alterations due to the plane, differ when the atom moves parallel to the mirror compared to the stationary case. Conversely, motion perpendicular to the plane has no impact on these spectral and lifetime properties. The primary mechanism behind these shifts is dynamical Stark mixing, which generates dipole moments proportional to the atom's velocity. Additional contributions arise from magnetic dipole radiation, though they cancel out in the perpendicular direction; in the collinear scenario, magnetic dipole shifts add constructively to electric dipole shifts enhanced by image-current effects. Consequently, the magnetic dipole contribution can enhance transition rates for head-on or retrograde collisions by up to 50%, while suppressing them by 50% in cases where the higher state's image is less excited than the ground state's image. Numerical evaluations confirm these shifts can increase transition probabilities by a factor of approximately 3. Our findings indicate that an atom's collision course with the mirror can induce significant modifications in spontaneous decay, even at mesoscopic velocities as low as 10 m/s. Furthermore, we show that our findings validate time-reversal symmetry in the master equation governing the density operator of the atom's internal degrees of freedom. Finally, we illustrate how our methodology can be extended to explain the frictional force acting on a stationary atom due to its coupling with an excited electronic state alongside the mirror. This scenario represents a form of dynamical Stark excitation driven by the mirror itself. We find that the induced permanent dipole moment scales with the square root of the transition frequency, leading to a frictional coefficient that exhibits a frequency dependence of $\omega^{5/2}$. The magnitude of this coefficient for an excited Rubidium atom is estimated to be approximately $10^{-29}$ kg/s. This scaling represents a distinctive signature of the mechanism, differentiating it from the conventional Casimir polarizability model, which predicts a stronger $\omega^3$ dependence. Conversely, at transition frequencies below a few picoseconds, the model predicts a frictional coefficient 100 times lower than the thermal Casimir model.

Observations of young stellar clusters often reveal numerous massive stars within compact regions with limited scatter in masses around $10 M_{\odot}$. However, the physical mechanisms capable of generating these specific observational signatures remain ambiguous. In this study, we utilized research version 3.0 of the BAZAN code to conduct numerous simulations varying key parameters, subsequently analyzing the resulting stellar mass spectra to identify those that replicate the observed characteristics. Across all simulations, we monitored the distribution of young stellar clusters within radii smaller than 0.1 pc to investigate their potential association with protostellar cores or dense molecular gas. These distributions exhibited power-law excesses at small radii with distinct breaks occurring between 0.02 and 0.05 pc. Furthermore, the simulations successfully accounted for an observed population of stars with varying ages up to 100 yr and mass spectra extending beyond $100 M_{\odot}$. This confirms that the BAZAN code can reproduce the features seen in the most massive star-forming regions. Additionally, many simulations indicated that the majority of stellar mass in small clusters ($R < 0.1$ pc) remains trapped within protostars, exhibiting distinct peaks in mass accretion for certain parameter configurations. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that the BAZAN code can replicate the key observational signatures of clusters hosting massive stars, thereby supporting a model in which massive stars form via the accretion onto protostars within a few years of each other. These findings also suggest that the proposed "massive star clumps" might actually represent high-density concentrations of protostars during the active accretion phase of large cluster structures. Consequently, our analysis indicates that the in situ formation and accretion scenarios for massive stars are compatible with current observational data. Consequently, templates must be extracted from source documents to enable effective document processing. We introduce PrintDoc dig, the most comprehensive printed document extraction tool to date, capable of handling documents formed by the combination of four basic elements in two-dimensional space: text, figures, tables, and layouts. Printed materials, whether handwritten or typed, vary greatly in format; therefore, print documents from the same category often share structural similarities. Leveraging these observations, we establish baseline rules for printing document extraction, while rule exceptions are addressed using machine learning. Our primary focus is text extraction given its critical nature; thus, we employ text detection models to locate characters while minimizing overlaps. Furthermore, textual information is classified based on the source document's print type using template extraction. Given the varied formats of printed documents, we generate features from local image patches to train a neural network for document classification. Additionally, we propose a printing method to reduce the volume of training data required. By enhancing feature robustness, this approach allows for effective classification with a smaller dataset. Although many printed documents are categorized into a limited set of print types, they exist across numerous formats within those types; therefore, we utilize sample documents from a few formats to train the neural network. This method yields a model that effectively classifies documents from unseen formats. Finally, we introduce a printing technique requiring only a small number of printed features, thereby reducing the need for large training datasets. Experiments were conducted on printed documents sourced from the ICDAR2017 Challenge Dataset. While our method does not cover all printed document types, it achieves excellent results with very few trained documents. The print doc dig tool is available at https://github.com/Mohamed-Elkady/PrintDoc_dig.

This paper introduces a novel channel estimator tailored for IEEE 802.11ad and beyond vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) links, which utilize massive multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems and beamformed transmission to achieve high throughput and robustness against channel impairments. The proposed estimator is computational-efficient, minimizing both time and energy consumption for practical implementation. By leveraging the sparsity of the channel impulse response (CIR) and the ability to isolate the direct line-of-sight (LoS) path through beam sweeping, the method accurately separates and estimates the LoS component even under severe non-LoS conditions. Since the majority of total channel energy resides in the LoS component, effectively cancelling it leaves residual residues with negligible energy. Consequently, the estimator achieves high accuracy with low computation cost by focusing solely on the LoS CIR component. Evaluation results demonstrate that this method efficiently extracts the LoS CIR and recovers it with a mean squared error of -70.1 dB. Furthermore, the estimated LoS component significantly enhances the coherence bandwidth of the channel impulse response. Overall, the estimator achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, particularly in very fast-moving scenarios.

Prior theoretical and experimental investigations have identified these waves in microwave and terahertz frequency ranges, demonstrating their emergence through a symmetric resistance transition from zero to infinity mid-spectrum. This study introduces a novel class of line waves termed cloaked line waves (CLWs), which propagate within a designated cloaking region generated by a metamaterial cloak capable of producing arbitrary field configurations beyond the dressing layer. The formulation of CLWs relies on the generalized transformation optics approach combined with coordinate mapping. To demonstrate this concept, a specific CLW mode is modeled within a rectangular metaslab cloak featuring a square central hole (representing the cloaking region) situated inside a uniform metaslab dressing layer. Spatially modulated CLW modes are theoretically predicted to exist within this cloaked region, offering significant potential for confining waves in areas seemingly inaccessible to conventional propagation methods. Furthermore, since the entire system remains lossless, these CLW modes exhibit no ohmic losses during transmission and maintain perfect polarization. Furthermore, because the entire apparatus operates without magnetic components, CLWs avoid terahertz-related challenges such as magnetic losses and complicated fabrication. Numerical simulations confirm the prediction of CLW modes and illustrate their arbitrary spatial configurations within the cloaking region. Additionally, these modes demonstrate robustness against defects in the metaslab cloak and hand-eye coordination effects. Finally, it is suggested that the proposed class of CLWs holds immense potential for various applications, including the routing and confining of terahertz waves in compact regions smaller than the wavelength and image sensing. This work thus lays the foundational theoretical framework for the future development and practical implementation of cloaked line waves.

This paper introduces a novel, data-efficient approach that eliminates the requirement for any labeled samples during adaptation. The method is achieved through the integration of two components. The first addresses downstream learning by adapting to two classes of interest—hot and cold—without utilizing labeled input. Instead, it leverages multiple stochastic estimators of each class to define revised assignment probabilities for unlabeled inputs. The second component implements a revision mechanism that adjusts these stochastic models to converge toward the true class distributions. This update process functions recursively to refine the assignment probabilities for unlabeled data. Consequently, downstream learning is continuously enhanced by repeatedly applying the hot-cold revision step using probabilistic models. Our approach is evaluated through two synthetic simulation studies and one empirical study. The findings demonstrate that the method successfully adapts to unlabeled data, rapidly converging to a solution comparable to one achievable with a small number of labeled samples. The goal is to create a systematic method for identifying factors that contribute to the digital exclusion of the elderly, with long-term ambitions of utilizing this data to foster inclusive technological environments. Potential applications span to personalized learning and professional training. The analysis focuses on three primary speech attributes: sentiment, style (characterized by robust or weak vocal quality), and robustness. Consequently, detecting shifts in speech characteristics through comparative analysis can offer insights into an elder's prior experience with smart speakers and their acceptance of the technology. Preliminary findings indicate that the speech of elders who have previously used smart speakers displays more neutral sentiment and softer vocal tones compared to those who have not yet had experience using the devices. While event detection has been extensively explored with strong performance, analyzing event streams remains underexplored. This approach often leads to duplication, as the same event generated by multiple users may be incorrectly classified as several different ones. This paper addresses that need by proposing a method to expand the feature vector of short social media posts using structural information extracted from user interaction networks. Leveraging this enhanced representation, we evaluate event detection accuracy and the correctness of the stream analysis. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves both detection precision and the correctness of analyzing event streams.

## 1 Introduction Reward learning is a highly effective framework for sample-efficient reinforcement learning from human feedback. State-action preference learning, which uses comparison labels, is a popular variant that has been widely adopted in both theoretical exploration and real-world applications. However, this approach suffers from two main issues: first, individual comparisons are costly for both computational resources and human annotators; second, the manual generation of each comparison label limits the model's ability to generalize from local decisions. We introduce the Reduced Dimensional Label Value Approximation RDLVA method, which is based on dimensionality reduction. RDLDA reduces the state space to two dimensions, creating two 2D grids where comparisons are aggregated into regions. This allows us to approximate comparison labels by evaluating entire regions instead of single instances. By reducing the number of required labels, we provide richer context, enabling RDLDA to learn more general policies with the same label count. Additionally, RDLDA can guide future comparisons by identifying areas of high value, directing annotators to the most informative comparisons. This framework offers a continuum between fully aggregated regions and single comparisons. At one extreme, the RDLDA method reduces the state space to two dimensions without requiring any individual comparison labels. At the other extreme, it recovers individual comparison labels. Our analysis centers on the coadjoint orbits within the area-preserving diffeomorphism group of ${\mathbb R}^2$ defined by these structures. We demonstrate that the corresponding polarization subgroup comprises diffeomorphisms that maintain the loop as a set; consequently, the resulting configuration space consists of loops enclosing a constant area, independent of the internal vorticity distribution or specific attachment points. Furthermore, we introduce a novel Hamiltonian mechanics framework for this system, featuring a singular hessian symmetric metric on the configuration space and an intrinsic geometric momentum map. The singular metric reveals an infinite-dimensional conformal family of equivalent metrics, with the Conformal Geometric Action (CGA) serving as a global scalar invariant. a causal parameter typically involves a two-step process: first, modeling the treatment and outcome while accounting for potential confounders; second, utilizing these predictions in ATE estimators like the Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW) method. Given concerns about bias and the trade-off between bias and variance, selection-based approaches have gained traction, introducing either a pre-treatment or post-treatment selection rule. While AIPW is unbiased under correct post-treatment selection, it exhibits high variance when the probability of treatment is low. Conversely, pre-treatment selection methods such as the Least Relevant Feature (LRF) method avoid this variance issue but risk conditioning on irrelevant variables and remain theoretically unproven. To overcome the limitations of both post- and pre-treatment methods, we introduce the Least Relevant Feature Selection (LRSF) estimator, which relies on pre-treatment selection but avoids conditioning on irrelevant ones. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of LRSF and demonstrate its superiority over LRF, BPRL, and AIPW through simulations. Furthermore, we validate our findings using data from an experiment conducted by the U.S. Personalized Learning Team. Additionally, to facilitate inference, we propose a data-driven screening method grounded in Conditional Minimax (CM) optimization, offering analytical guarantees along with an efficient algorithm. Numerical results indicate that this new method effectively identifies significant variables for consistency while discovering highly relevant features for the ATE problem that LRSF can leverage. Finally, we provide robustness evidence for both LRSF and the CM-based screening approach. Our code is accessible at the provided link. a crucial role in the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model, primarily due to its significantly larger mass compared to muons and its extensive collection of data from the LEP $e^+e^-$ collider. This paper outlines a method to measure the fractional contribution of decays into new physics particles within $\tau$ lepton final states. Derived using only conservation laws, this fractional measurement can be achieved through studies of individual decay channels, combinations of these channels, or the total decay width. Consequently, it serves as a valuable lower-level diagnostic tool for the LCLS $\tau$ factory. Additionally, the study examines how this technique applies to each decay channel, evaluates their respective sensitivities, and analyzes the impacts of new physics contributions and other uncertainties. Finally, we outline the required LCLS $\tau$ factory parameters to conduct these diagnostics during the initial years of operation. With an assumed annual integrated luminosity of $\mathcal{L}=100\,\mathrm{pb}^{-1}$, the sensitivity of the fractional measurement in the future LCLS $\tau$ factory reaches approximately 0.1%. This corresponds to the ability to detect new physics contributions to the existing Standard Model particles in $\tau$ decays at the $5\sigma$ level if the fraction reaches the 0.5% level, or to exclude new physics contributions in the range of $[0,0.3]\%$ at the 95% confidence level. These objectives are feasible within two years of operation at the proposed LCLS $\tau$ factory. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed LCLS $\tau$ factory has the potential to explore a new physics scale of up to $\sqrt{E_{NP}}\sim$ 5 TeV. Furthermore, the developed technique for measuring new physics fractions in $\tau$ decays is also applicable to other heavy particles, including the $B_c$ meson, $D_s$ meson, and $K$ meson. Supporting this, we provide examples illustrating the sensitivity of this approach for the $B_c$ meson. Given that the $B_c$ meson is produced in an abundant sample at the LCLS $\tau$ factory, similar analyses could be conducted in the future.

We present numerical simulations of this system at moderate aspect ratios under periodic boundary conditions, utilizing a novel spectral collocation method tailored for periodic domains with non-matching spatial scales. These simulations reveal the spontaneous symmetry breaking characteristic of the system, giving rise to traveling wave patterns. This symmetry breaking occurs via a subcritical bifurcation, which makes the system sensitive to minor perturbations. The resulting patterns consist of traveling waves confined to an annular sector, propagating in both directions with varying amplitudes. Depending on the rotation speed and temperature gradient, the amplitude of two dominant meridional modes oscillates temporally. Through both spectral and time analysis, multiple states are identified where the system remains locked in a persistent pattern, dynamically stabilizing a single dominant mode. The corresponding pressure fields generate steady east-west overturning flows within the annulus. Furthermore, the stability periods of these persistent states decrease as rotation speed increases and as thermal gradients adopt lower aspect ratios. This behavioral profile mirrors that observed in larger-scale atmospheric baroclinic wave systems. Consequently, our findings suggest that setting up and maintaining the rotating annulus experiment with moderate parameters, along with analyzing the resulting flow using pressure sensors or visualization techniques, could reliably produce steady traveling patterns with varying amplitudes. Such outcomes would be readily comparable to existing wind tunnel experiments or laser-induced fluorescence data from the rotating annulus facility. However, this model's validity relies on the threshold being sufficiently high, which complicates parameter estimation because the true threshold level is unknown. We propose addressing this validity check through a Bayesian framework that incorporates a discrete uniform prior over a finite set of potential thresholds. In a setting where an adversary can arbitrarily alter an $\epsilon$ fraction of the state-action-reward-next-state tuples in a batch dataset, the learner's objective is to derive a near-optimal policy while accessing only the uncorrupted data. We first demonstrate that without any assumptions on the adversary's behavior beyond the bound on $\epsilon$, even simple deterministic environments become unsolvable. Consequently, we introduce two distinct adversary models to define feasible problems. The initial model necessitates that the adversary act non-adversarially toward future outcomes, meaning admissible datasets must be statistically consistent with some uncorrupted transition distribution; the second model further constrains the adversary to modify only one component of each tuple. For online learning under general position distributions, we establish that the minimax optimal sample complexity is $\Theta(1/\epsilon + \text{pol}(\log(1/\epsilon)))$. Leveraging recent results indicating that near-optimal policies are learnable in polynomial time when the dataset originates from a pure self-play distribution, we show that both tasks are solvable in polynomial time. Our first offline algorithm achieves polynomial sample complexity of $\Theta(\text{poly}(\log(1/\epsilon)))$, which is near-optimal up to logarithmic factors and matches the upper bound of the online problem. Our second algorithm exhibits complexity $\Theta(\text{poly}(\log(1/\epsilon)^2))$, matching the established lower bound of the problem. Our proof methodology relies on a technique of analyzing learning complexity through the lens of statistical query complexity, alongside the construction of hard instances using random continuous Gaussian functions. These continuous random functions serve as the first instance construction of this kind in reinforcement learning. Furthermore, our results provide a route to addressing adversarial robustness in offline learning for other function classes, such as neural networks, by utilizing existing robust query complexity results. In summary, our contributions include the first rigorous formalization of adversarial attacks in offline reinforcement learning, the first feasible assumptions on adversarial attacks, near-optimal complexity results for polynomial time learnability, and the first use of random continuous Gaussian functions to establish tight complexity bounds. Lastly, we offer a high-level discussion on the implications of these findings for deep learning.

As a result, we demonstrate impulse approximate controllability for the impulsive heat equation under similar dynamic boundary constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit upper limit for the cost associated with impulse control. Finally, we provide a constructive algorithm to calculate the impulsive control with the minimal $L^2$-norm, accompanied by numerical experiments that verify the theoretical findings and illustrate the algorithm's efficiency. We demonstrate boundary observability for the fractional heat equation on the interval $(0,1)$ by reducing the problem to finite-time internal observability in a higher-dimensional setting. This approach relies on a criterion concerning the decay rate of eigenfunctions for the fractional Laplacian within a finite domain. Consequently, we approximate the boundary observability constant using a finite number of eigenfunctions and derive an explicit upper bound for the corresponding boundary control norm in $L^2(0,T)$. We prove this estimate is sharp for control times $T > (2k+1)\pi/\pi_{\mathbb{R}}$, provided $k$ is sufficiently large, by demonstrating the necessary conditions for the associated spectral estimate to hold. Finally, we examine the limit as $s$ approaches 1 in the observability inequality and show that the boundary control norm for the classical heat equation can be bounded above by the sum of finitely many series, each composed of transcendental functions. In this context, we illustrate the approximation of the boundary control norm for specific values of $\nu$ in $L^2(0,T)$ and present numerical simulations verifying our theoretical findings.

We establish the existence and uniqueness of a global-in-time mild solution for a stochastic semilinear parabolic equation influenced by boundary noise. Furthermore, we derive a mean square exponential decay estimate for this solution. Regarding the long-term behavior, we demonstrate the existence of a unique random attractor consisting of continuously deformable bounded random sets and provide an estimate for its fractal dimension. Finally, we investigate the normal attractor and its related attributes in the context of the stochastic semilinear Laplace equation.

We propose a unified framework that (1) categorizes OOD definitions based on their underlying assumptions and (2) evaluates the impact of these variations on detection algorithms. Leveraging the long-range electrostatic interactions characteristic of material surfaces, these systems can be driven by external electric field bias. This work demonstrates the design, synthesis, and operation of a new class of molecular assemblies for surface integration, utilizing conductive gold (111) surfaces as a critical component. The study reveals that the classically entangled structure of a chiral acid derivative is destabilized by surface-induced forces, streamlining assembly into a helical morphology and facilitating surface activation. Overall, this research highlights the unique potential of chiral organic molecular assemblies on conductive surfaces to serve as efficient, energy-effective motors. These findings open new avenues for integrating molecular assemblies into electronically controllable nanoscale devices. This paper presents an additional decidability result concerning transducers that approximate one-way transducers within the origin semantics framework. Specifically, we demonstrate that it is decidable whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an origin-equivalent one-way transducer via resynchronization by a bounded, regular resynchronizer. This finding contrasts sharply with standard semantics, where determining if a non-deterministic two-way transducer is equivalent to any one-way transducer remains undecidable. Our proof strategy adapts the word equation approach, previously used to resolve several origin-related decidability questions, to the setting of origin-synchronizing transducers. Consequently, we establish that it is also decidable whether the (origin-)synchronization distance between two origin-synchronizing transducers is finite. Furthermore, we prove that for any two origin-synchronizing transducers, there exists a resynchronizer capable of reducing their synchronization distance by a specified amount within origin semantics. Leveraging these results, we further demonstrate that it is decidable whether the synchronization distance between two origin-synchronizing transducers is finite. Finally, we provide multiple examples of languages and transducers highlighting the distinctities and insights offered by our work, as well as the challenges inherent in this domain. Overall, our results stand in opposition to standard semantics and open up numerous new research directions.

first T-dwarf, GJ 229B has been the subject of extensive study for nearly three decades due to its unique nature as a cool companion star emitting most of its radiation in the infrared. Recent advancements in high spectral resolution near-infrared spectroscopy have revealed the presence of strong stellar winds on its surface, characterized by H-I absorption. Despite this extensive research, the source of stellar activity driving these winds remains unidentified. To investigate whether magnetic fields are responsible, we conducted new low-resolution spectroscopic observations using the LASCP/HPF instrument on the GTC in March 2022. Our analysis of the resulting spectra successfully identified several high-order stellar activity lines. Furthermore, data from the HST/STIS archive were employed to search for these same lines during observations from 1999 and 2001. Although the detection of these lines confirms the presence of magnetic fields, the variability of their intensity suggests an apsidal motion period of significantly less than 100 years. This finding indicates that GJ 229B's period has been changing since its initial detection in the early 2000s, a trajectory that predicts an increase in its period by approximately 2 years based on current data. We propose that the stellar field within the GJ 229 system may be responsible for this behavior. Furthermore, we explore the possibility that the interaction between stellar winds and an accretion disk could explain the unique evolution of GJ 229B. Finally, these observations represent the most detailed studies conducted to date on the stellar activity levels of T-dwarfs.

Nevertheless, existing models largely overlook the influence of breath dynamics on these aerosol particles. This study introduces a novel model that integrates the effects of breathing patterns and respiration flow between infected and uninfected persons, alongside breakage and coalescence of aerosols from infected breath plumes. Questionnaires administered to 1,382 adults regarding their respiratory and other health symptoms revealed a distinct association between HEPA air cleaning and the reduction of specific symptoms, most notably coughing. This study sought to correlate particulate matter (PM) removal efficiency with cough reduction by analyzing data from a randomized controlled trial published in JAMA Internal Medicine (Sullivan et al., 2019). We developed a systematic approach to estimate theoretical uncertainties by comparing model predictions with experimental data. Within each mass region, we calculated $\chi^2$ values by assessing the discrepancies between observed and calculated values for decay energy, log ft values, and angular correlation coefficients, while also incorporating model-to-experimental rate uncertainties. The resulting Large-$F$ large-$N$ (L-F L-N) space-spanning force served as a functional fit to an existing force in the same energy space. This new L-F L-N force yields $\beta$-decay properties that are approximately 30% closer to experimental values compared to the original large-space force. Furthermore, the improved calculation demonstrates that the L-F L-N space-spanning force can effectively bridge different model spaces. Notably, the optimized forces achieve root mean square (RMS) errors of 0.131 and 0.044 for decay energy, and 0.133 and 0.101 for log ft values, respectively, without sacrificing the overall quality of the fit relative to the original large-space forces. Additionally, we investigated binding energy calculations and found that the L-F L-N force yields a smaller RMS error of 3.33 MeV, indicating better agreement with A$\beta$-Base masses than the original large-space force. Finally, by examining $\beta$-decay data from A$\beta$-Base, we addressed the charge independence violation (CIV) energy and its correlation with neutron excess ($N-Z$). These findings provide a fresh perspective on the relationship between CIV and log ft. We demonstrate that, unlike the standard quantized Hall effect, this phenomenon does not rely on Landau level formation or carrier confinement two dimensions. Using an effective model for interacting electrons coupled to optical phonons, we investigate transport properties in three-dimensional systems with random potential strong-coupling regimes. While transport remains diffusive, we find that electron-phonon interactions induce anomalous corrections to conductivity in the 1/$_\omega$ power of frequency, leading to extreme behavior at low temperatures. Based on these findings, we propose a physical mechanism for the observed anomalous conductivity decay in thick copper films. Finally, we discuss the potential experimental observation of this effect and its relevance to mysterious conductivity behaviors reported in other disordered metal-film systems.

We introduce a general framework for analyzing the coupled dynamics of gauge and scalar fields that includes a polynomial interaction term $\lambda^{int}\Phi^n$. This formalism utilizes an auxiliary field to decompose the original potential into a sum of marginal potentials, each possessing classical scaling dimensions. We calculate the complete one-loop $\beta$ functions for the resulting marginally coupled system across various dimensions and analyze the infrared fixed points. Our results indicate that marginal interactions can drive marginal theories toward nontrivial infrared fixed points in $d=3$ and $d=4$. Given that marginal deformations are central to the conformal bootstrap approach to strongly coupled theories, our findings suggest a path to explore a broader landscape of strongly coupled theories. We also examine marginal theories coupled to a nearly conformal topological term, finding that marginal couplings can influence the running of the nearly conformal theory. This work provides a foundation for future research into marginal deformations of non-free theories and for systematically analyzing marginal operators in the conformal bootstrap program. This paper complements our simultaneous study of marginally relevant deformations.

While Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) has emerged as a powerful data-driven technique for linear dynamics, it fails to capture the full spectrum of behaviors in high-dimensional, unknown nonlinear systems. To overcome this, we introduce a novel approach called Koopman operator learning with feature selection (KFS). Specifically, we develop a new algorithm that utilizes feature selection as an interpretable mechanism for supervising the training of a nonlinear Koopman operator. Experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques and effectively recovers various dynamical features from synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, by reframing KFS as a cooperative game, we derive an interpretable probabilistic interpretation of the Koopman operator's structure, thereby establishing a robust theoretical foundation for this critical discovery. Finally, we discuss how the proposed methodology enhances predictive modeling across several domains, including supply chain management and renewable energy systems.

Specifically, the agent successfully discovered new games in the Reti, London, and King's Indian defenses within days. Designed to generate legal chess moves, the agent was intentionally restricted from discovering new openings; consequently, all subsequent games featured by the agent adhered to established opening rules. Nevertheless, the agent consistently produced unusual but legal moves, often classified as blunders by humans. Nevertheless, these atypical moves frequently led to checkmate within a few turns. Our findings indicate that despite its limited knowledge, the agent demonstrated an exceptional ability to construct efficient attack paths. Furthermore, we observed that the agent's deep networks effectively functioned as piece evaluators, achieving an accuracy of approximately 80%. Ultimately, our work illustrates how deep reinforcement learning can effectively address complex problems defined by simple yet strict rules. While our approach does not compete with human grandmasters regarding game length or overall strategy, it excels at uncovering new games and attacking sequences. Consequently, this study offers a distinctive and powerful alternative to computer-assisted grandmaster analyses, which typically prioritize board evaluation rather than move generation. By highlighting the value of unexpected yet legal moves, our work presents a unique supplement to established opening databases. Furthermore, we demonstrate how specialized agents can enhance exploration in reinforcement learning. All discovered games are available on our dedicated website, which also provides detailed game annotations. Furthermore, our comprehensive online repository includes the source code for training agents across various state-space problems of increasing complexity, as well as the data used in this study. Finally, to facilitate the discovery of new games by others, we have released a specialized agent tool.

Initially, these phase transitions were documented in the context of pattern formation among periodic solutions, where the breakage of spatial symmetry upon transition earned them the label "symmetry-breaking." More recently, dynamical phase transitions have been identified in almost-periodic solutions, characterized by the disruption of both spatial and temporal symmetries. In this work, we administer a comprehensive statistical analysis to pinpoint the specific spatial and temporal symmetry-breaking events that constitute the algebraic mechanism underlying the global occurrence of symmetry-breaking phase transitions across all non-equilibrium solution types. Furthermore, by establishing the morphological relationship between temporal symmetry breakage in almost-periodic solutions and spatial symmetry breakage in periodic solutions, we can unify the description of all non-equilibrium symmetry-breaking phenomena under a single framework. Consequently, the term "symmetry-breaking" is now recognized as an analogy that comprehensively encapsulates all non-equilibrium manifestations of spatial and temporal symmetry breakage across diverse spatial-temporal solution types. Concomitantly, the description of all non-equilibrium symmetry-breaking phenomena evolves from a fragmented state, previously characterized by isolated individual studies, into a coherent, system-wide understanding grounded in mathematics. This research also clarifies a longstanding misconception found in existing literature. Constructing upon this mathematical coherence, we show how to determine the morphological characteristics of all non-equilibrium symmetry-breaking phenomena through a unified algebraic mechanism known as the lattice-breaking mechanism. Consequently, the lattice-breaking mechanism establishes an intrinsic notion of "symmetry" for dynamical solutions that is entirely distinct from the description-based notion previously employed in earlier studies. Leveraging the lattice-breaking mechanism, we can describe all non-equilibrium symmetry-breaking phenomena not via scattered individual studies, but as a single coherent phenomenon characterized by its specific temporal and spatial periods, its unique morphological nature, and its specific manifestation type derived from various mathematical mechanisms renowned across numerous other contexts. Leveraging these theories enables the development of a universally applicable statistical framework for the global detection of all non-equilibrium symmetry-breaking phenomena based on full-order time series data for arbitrary spatial-temporal solutions, regardless of their specific equilibrium status, symbolic representation, morphological nature, or manifestation type. Applying this framework yields a simultaneously partitioning and classification functional manifold decomposition of the global statistical landscape regarding all non-equilibrium symmetry-breaking phenomena associated with a specific physical system. Additionally, the manifold components can be characterized quantitatively and interpreted qualitatively using a universal symbolic language derived from the representation theory applicable to all spatial-temporal symmetries.

This paper introduces a novel method for learning to extract table conditions using a new dataset comprising 349 tables with corresponding conditions. Condition extraction involves identifying visual elements within a table, such as rows, columns, or cells, that convey important information for a specific context. We review several prominent arguments found in the literature that justify the necessity of complex formalism and offer additional insights by introducing alternative perspectives. Our goal is to reinforce the challenging pedagogical task of explaining why Quantum Mechanics requires complex numbers. In this endeavor, we adopt a non-relativistic framework and provide several alternative approaches to address the problem. In contrast to other frameworks commonly presented, we rely primarily on physical principles rather than quantum formalism. Specifically, we frame the problem as one of constructing a quantum theory from a set of guiding physical principles. To enhance understanding, we begin by outlining the physical arguments that motivate our approach. Subsequently, we present a mathematical formulation for each problem, grounded in the physical reasoning described. In most instances, our formulation relies on the path integral concept and assumes only linearity. It emerges that these two principles—path integrals and linearity—are sufficient to derive the quantum nature of a system, even though we do not explicitly invoke complex numbers or complex amplitudes in our initial setup. Furthermore, we demonstrate that complex numbers are inherently indispensable in quantum theory by examining the specific functions they perform, a characteristic distinct from our other approaches. In conclusion, our framework not only avoids relying on the quantum postulate to explain the necessity of complex numbers but also elucidates the specific tasks they undertake within the theory. Given that our formulation relies on concepts as intuitive as the path integral, this work reinforces the claim that complex numbers do provide an elegant and powerful formalism for Quantum Mechanics, as established by other approaches, but this elegance is not merely a lucky coincidence. Finally, we highlight that formulating a quantum theory based on these two intuitive principles represents an alternative starting point for developing a theory of quantum systems, potentially proving beneficial in quantum foundations and, possibly, in the formulation of a quantum theory of gravity. Additionally, we provide an overview of other approaches based on relativistic considerations. A comprehensive detail for each method is beyond the scope of this work, as the objective is to illustrate the diversity of perspectives through which the quantum nature of a system can be intuitively understood. Finally, we examine other physical principles that are not immediately obvious but remain fundamental to nature, aiming to inspire further research on the grounding of a quantum theory based on these principles. Overall, we believe that presenting various approaches serves to strengthen the argument regarding the necessity of complex numbers and reinforces the effort to build a theory from principles that feel more natural to a physicist. Running artificial neural networks on simulated neuromorphic systems via virtual platforms (VPs) is computationally intensive, yet it remains a critical benchmarking step for comparing architectural alternatives. Consequently, leveraging the multicore capabilities of the VP's host hardware is essential for accelerating simulations. This paper introduces a parallel SystemC-based VP tailored for RISC-V multicore platforms that integrate multiple computing-in-memory neuromorphic accelerators. Furthermore, it examines various VP segmentation architectures for integrating these accelerators and demonstrates their performance gains through speedup simulations relative to traditional sequential SystemC execution. Utilizing MCSTF's multicore RISC-V virtual platform, we achieved a 5.4x simulation speedup compared to sequential SystemC modeling. By comparing different parallel SystemC methodologies, we found that a coarse-grained VP architecture yielded superior results, offering seven times faster performance than other parallel approaches. These findings aim to guide future research in simulating and deploying advanced, complex, and heterogeneous MCSTF-like computing-in-memory architectures on RISC-V multicore systems. To support reproducibility, the VP source code, build scripts, and RISC-V binaries for MCSTF-based SPNNs are publicly available at https://mcstf-project.org/vp/. MCSTF represents a novel class of spiking neural network accelerators designed for low latency, high throughput, high fidelity, and high computing-in-memory intensity. To date, no existing VP or simulator adequately captures the nuanced behaviors of these high-fidelity memory devices, nor does any available VP model their interaction within RISC-V computing systems. Therefore, a detailed analysis of the proposed VP's granularity is necessary. This work also analyzes the overheads of VP simulation and their impact on the overall speedup achieved. These elements collectively demonstrate how a VP for RISC-V multicore platforms with multiple MCSTF accelerators can significantly enhance simulation speeds as RISC-V adoption rises.

However, because deep learning models function as opaque black boxes, researchers turn to explainers to make them transparent. Despite the existence of numerous methods for interpreting deep learning models, comparing them remains difficult due to a lack of standard evaluation metrics. To address this gap, the SHAPLEY game theory-based Interpretability Metric (SHAPIM) was proposed, serving as the first metric to quantify the explanatory power of deep learning models across general use cases. While many existing metrics are limited to specific tasks, SHAPIM offers a universal framework applicable to diverse architectures and methodologies across various domains. Nevertheless, its practical application has been hindered by the absence of a robust evaluation protocol, as prior metrics suffer from inherent flaws. This study introduces the first rigorous evaluation protocol for SHAPIM using reverse engineering techniques. We demonstrate that SHAPIM can assess explanatory power for the most prevalent approaches in literature, thereby fostering comparison and advancement of new techniques within a standardized, practical framework. The evaluation reveals that SHAPIM successfully enhances interpretability, understanding, and trust in deep learning models, acting as a reliable tool for researchers in the field. The implementation of SHAPIM is publicly available at https://github.com/NourhanMahmoud/Shapley-Interpretability-Metric-and-its-Evaluation. This study demonstrates the successful fabrication of polytype III-V semiconductors, specifically InP, which form twisted nanosheets along the [110] direction relative to the underlying graphene. These structures display atomic rows maintaining a constant interatomic distance, indicating that the nanoparticles develop in an epirelaxation state on the graphene substrate. High-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy confirms that the nanoparticles' valence and conduction bands align with the expected ternary semiconductor configuration. We anticipate that this approach will facilitate the growth of various other materials with substantial lattice mismatches, including various III-V and II-VI semiconductors, perovskites, oxides, and nitrides. Furthermore, this methodology paves the way for creating new membrane-based devices, such as memristors and light-emitting diodes, based on III-V materials. This abundance of luminous galaxies, highly dependent on the specific line-of-sight, cannot be explained by standard galaxy evolution models. Various hypotheses were assessed against the full spectral energy distribution (SED) of these bright galaxies; while most suggest only minor enhancements in very bright galaxy populations, they all require an unphysical increase in the number of highly luminous galaxies throughout the merger history. Consequently, we conclude that the sheer number of very bright sources and their diverse SEDs observed in El Gordo's core indicate that these galaxies are spatially separated despite appearing overlapped in projection. This arrangement is likely caused by the complex, turbulent gravitational environment of the merging cluster, which prevents significant radial redistribution of the galaxies. Furthermore, assuming these galaxies are physically distinct rather than spatially overlapped would fundamentally alter the interpretation of cosmic-web observations relying on source counts and luminosity functions. Finally, considering that approximately 80% of El Gordo's enhanced X-ray emission originates from within the same region as the bright source overdensity reinforces the idea that these galaxies remain physically separated within the turbulent intracluster medium. Although the Content Industry Alliance (CIA), designed to distribute these profits, has existed theoretically since 2004, its implementation remains unresolved. This paper models the CIA as a game-theoretic framework where a social welfare function represents the total profit shared between CPs and ISPs. We analyze the existence of equilibria under a general utility function applicable to both ISP monopolies and oligopolies. Furthermore, we examine the impact of the allocation ratio—dividing profits between CPs and ISPs—and explore VOD market scenarios where ISPs invest in interconnection capacity to access competing content. Numerical experiments illustrate these results, and we conclude by discussing potential extensions. Our primary finding shows that allocating a high proportion of revenue to ISPs, rather than Content Providers, is suboptimal for both players and the market as a whole.

We compare representative exponential and polynomial $\alpha$-attractor models against the most recent cosmological datasets (Planck' 18 combined with BICEP2/Keck array) to derive parameter predictions and best-fit values. This analysis was conducted using ModeChord and CosmoMC, integrated through PolyChord. Our findings indicate that the exponential $\alpha$-attractor model is strongly favored by the Planck' 18 dataset, while both the Planck 2018 best-inflation dataset and the Planck' 18 + BICEP2/Keck array constraints favor the exponential model over the polynomial version. We note that relaxing the dark energy equation of state parameter from a fixed value of $w=0$ to a free parameter shifts the best-fit values for both models to slightly larger $r$ values. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these polynomial models can be quantitatively transformed into fibred inflation models, thereby allowing our results to inform future studies of fibred inflation. Finally, considering parameter extensions such as the curvature perturbation $\mathcal{R}$ and the tensor-to-scalar ratio $G\mathcal{R}^2$, the polynomial $\alpha$-attractor models remain strongly preferred. Let $\lambda$ denote a transverse measure for a measured foliation $[\mathfrak{f}]$ defined on the closed surface $S$ with genus $g \geq 2$. Through the identification established by Takhtajan and Zograf, the space $\mathcal{M}_g$ of such transverse measures possesses the structure of a Euclidean space with a specific constant dimension. This study demonstrates that the mapping from $\mathcal{M}_g$ to the quasi-Fuchsian space $\mathcal{QF}(S)$, which sends a transverse measure $\lambda$ to its associated measured foliation $[\mathfrak{f}]$ situated at infinity, constitutes an immersion. In the context of a handlebody group, the mapping represents a genuine immersion only when the handlebody projection complex exhibits no three-edges. Additionally, we explore the characteristics of such immersions by presenting examples and conjectures indicating when the differential fails to maintain full rank. adaptive sensory systems characterized by nonlinear transduction and novel plasticity. Sensory systems serve as the initial link in an information flow chain connecting the external world to higher cortical brain areas. While the traditional engineering approach focuses on ideal linear time-invariant (LTI) filters to derive optimal linear encoding strategies—which have been experimentally observed in the larval zebrafish visual system—our proposed biological nonlinear system diverges significantly from this classical framework.

In contrast to the standard engineering method, which assumes a fixed forward channel, in our computational model, both the forward sensory pathway and the subsequent decoding process at the brain are allowed to optimally co-adapt based on the statistical properties of natural stimuli. Leveraging the principle of detailed balance, we formulate an optimal nonlinear encoding scheme and computationally identify a robust, efficient encoding strategy for the adapted system. Exploiting the visual system's inherent rotational symmetry, we represent both nonlinear encoders and LTI decoders as Rosenblatt neurons, a class of neural elements that are biologically superior to their linear equivalents.

Experimental results reveal that this proposed nonlinear Rosenblatt neuron achieves over 20% higher efficiency than the traditional linear optimal filter when processing natural images. Furthermore, our nonlinear Rosenblatt neurons demonstrate superior resilience to adaptation-induced changes in the visual stimulus distribution compared to linear models, suggesting a basis for the observed robustness in developing zebrafish visual systems. Overall, our nonlinear Rosenblatt neurons offer biological advantages over linear linear optimal filters, including lower implementation costs and novel, computable plasticity-based learning rules that guide the system toward optimality. These findings offer a basis for re-evaluating the mechanisms behind emerging nonlinear processing strategies in visual systems. Keywords: Nonlinear transduction, Rosenblatt neuron, Optimal encoding/decoding, Optimal co-adaptation, Plasticity.

Mathematics & Statistics has aimed to cultivate an inclusive and welcoming environment for all students pursuing mathematics. Historically, our strategy to address the lack of diversity in our majors focused on remediation, attempting to fix perceived student deficits through specific programming. However, in recent years, we have shifted to an anti-deficit approach that prioritizes transforming the department itself. The initiatives detailed below reflect this shift, designed to strengthen community, foster collaboration, and improve the overall climate within our department.

Our core philosophy is straightforward: we must stop asking students to adapt to us and instead commit to making our own institution fit for them. We believe that, like any other institution, our department possesses the power to choose its attitude. All of the following initiatives were proposed and finalized during our first year (Fall 2019 to Spring 2020) serving on the New Advisory Committee. We, the five New Advisory Committee members, are eager to support and champion these initiatives as an acting collective. Furthermore, we welcome any additional proposals from our colleagues, students, or others, as we are dedicated to collaborating with everyone to make our department an excellent place to learn mathematics.

Specific initiatives include:

**PAC-MAT Speaker Series**
To broaden the scope of topics presented in our departmental speaker series, we established the PAC-MAT (Pomona College Advocates for a Changed/Improved Mathematics Department) Speaker Series. This program invites speakers from an expansive array of careers and activities, including research, high school teaching, summer research mentorship, laboratory work, professional associations, and student outreach. Various members of the New Advisory Committee will help organize and publicize these events over the coming year. Additionally, each speaker will receive a one-on-one mentorship opportunity, allowing our committee to directly engage with and learn from our visitors.

**Anti Deficit Implicit Bias Training** Implicit bias plays a significant role in our actions and perceptions. Last year, our committee researched and contacted various anti-deficit training providers. Last spring, we drafted a proposal for the Mathematics Department Faculty Meeting to initiate these trainings. Last fall, we worked with appropriate administrators to secure funding and schedule the sessions. Last spring, we coordinated the logistics and served as the primary point of contact for the implicit bias training series. This year, we plan to host two training sessions during our Departmental Diversity Committee meeting, ensuring broad participation from across the department. These sessions will be led by our department's appointed Diversity and Inclusion Coordinators, allowing for a more intensive and personalized

Participants underwent a virtual hand immersion task where they could apply virtual pressure to a moving obstacle, resulting in either a painful pinch or a non-painful touch. The analysis revealed that the absence of predicted pain caused participants to underestimate risks by a factor of three and significantly reduced their vigilance regarding environmental hazards. This study investigates how readers' questions affect attention, reading speed, memory, and the ability to identify previously unresolved questions. Through two online experiments involving computer science students and early-career researchers, we manipulated the questions readers held before reading a security paper. Experiment 1 featured 112 participants who answered either technical or non-technical questions before engaging with the material. Experiment 2 involved 109 participants responding to questions of similar types but written in more complex language. Results indicated that the type of pre-study question guided attention toward relevant content. However, regardless of the question type, readers struggled to resolve issues or questions prior to reading. Additionally, answering more complex questions led to slower reading times. These findings suggest that readers may select inappropriate questions to guide their reading, implying a potential benefit to providing researchers with key information before they read a paper. Finally, indicating information did not impact reading time. The study's materials are accessible at https://osf.io/5g55u/.

Both simulations display characteristic time-varying accretion and ejection masses along the z-axis at the center of the progenitor, confirming the presence of the NRAB cycle (neutrino-driven convection and radial instabilities). In the two-vapor-phase convection scenario, the cold debris generated by multiple vapor-phase shells amplifies the instabilities, triggering fast flavor instabilities within the amplification zone. These instabilities occur at a distance exceeding 100 km from the proto-neutron star center, significantly farther than the boundary of the accretion column. Conversely, in the single-vapor-phase case, an early fast flavor instability occurs at distances under 100 km from the proto-neutron star center during an ejection phase. These findings suggest that fast flavor instabilities can arise at locations significantly distant from the proto-neutron star center if the amplification conditions are met. Furthermore, the fast flavor instabilities observed correlate with fluctuations in electron-type neutrino antineutrino asymmetry ($\tilde A_{\overline{\nu}_e}$). This work marks the first identification of fast flavor instabilities in core-collapse supernova simulations using state-of-the-art neutrino transport and hydrodynamic treatments of the neutrino-driven mechanism. The identified instabilities may substantially influence the electron-to-positron ratio in ejected neutrinos and the properties of supernova ejecta. Additionally, these instabilities may offer an explanation for the physical scales seen in DSNB (Daya Bay) data and could represent a novel flavor conversion mechanism for astrophysical neutron star mergers and accretion onto black holes. Given that several analyses searching for flavor non-conservation in supernova explosions are either ongoing or planned, a detailed investigation of fast flavor instabilities in supernova explosions is timely and necessary. Finally, if MHD turbulence can prevent the formation of cold debris and suppress the cold-spot amplification effect, it could suppress these fast flavor instabilities inside the accretion column. These results highlight the significance of investigating the interplay between neutrino-driven convection, instabilities, and particle-phase phenomena for the development of constitutive equations in supernova simulations. These findings may also serve as a novel diagnostic for identifying instabilities

While self-reported symptoms offer an alternative approach that is increasingly supported by emerging evidence, the specific role of inattention versus hyperactivity is still unclear. To address this, researchers utilize large-scale datasets combining genetic and phenotypic data to examine the comorbidity structure of these symptoms. This study analyzes the research methodology and key findings regarding the comorbidity of ADHD symptoms, examining how different analytical approaches influence the resulting conclusions. The computational methodology for modeling symptom comorbance from genetic and phenotypic data involves estimating research outcomes as functions of these variables. Given the intractability of such estimation, methodological advancements have been essential. Currently, attention and activity are modeled separately as binary traits using standard machine learning techniques like Support Vector Machines (SVMS) or Logistic Regression (LR). Effect sizes from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) are subsequently employed to deconvolve the polygenic architecture and derive phenotypic parameters, a process known as deconvolution. Another proposed method utilizes a Bayesian approach to jointly estimate model parameters and effect sizes directly from GWAS data. Both deconvolution and joint estimation methods yield similar insights into the comorbidity pattern of ADHD symptoms. However, differences exist in the estimated patterns and the complexity of the comorbance model derived from phenotypic data. These variations stem from assumptions made during the estimation process and the order in which operations are performed. Ultimately, this analysis highlights the methodological landscape of ADHD comorbance research and provides evidence-informed recommendations for interpreting existing literature. Furthermore, it serves as a practical guide for implementing these methodologies across various software environments, including R and Python. By enabling researchers to leverage large-scale genetic and phenotypic datasets through accessible and reproducible methods, this work advances our understanding of ADHD comorbidity structures. This paper aims to summarize these methodological advancements and provide evidence supporting the direction for future research. Furthermore, it offers an implementation guide utilizing the ADHDcombin R package across different software environments. Finally, future research should explore more refined estimation methods and utilize joint models to maximize the value of large-scale genetic and phenotypic data for comprehensively characterizing ADHD comorbance.
